summary: Kerman sits on the dead-flat floor of the San Joaquin Valley about fifteen miles west of Fresno, and its 3.3 square miles pack in roughly 5,274 people per square mile — denser than many California suburbs twice its size, yet the horizon line stretches unbroken in every direction across irrigated farmland. Agriculture is the economic engine here and across the surrounding region: packing houses, almond orchards, and dairy operations generate the jobs that keep the town running, which means employment options are tightly clustered around a single industry rather than spread across competing sectors. The median home value of $331,500 against a median household income of $57,556 yields a price-to-income ratio near 5.8 — more accessible than coastal California but still a stretch, and with a quarter of households below the poverty line, ownership is out of reach for a significant share of the population. Summers are punishing: average daily highs push well above 90°F from June through September under 9.4 hours of sun, while winters are mild and tule-fog-draped. With a poverty rate of 25.3% and limited retail variety, Kerman functions less as a self-contained town and more as an agricultural satellite where affordable housing and relentless Central Valley sunshine come packaged with a long Fresno commute for anyone working outside the farm economy.
